requirements.text: The applicant must describe how rainwater will be stored on site and state the total storage capacity in litres that is planned.
The applicant must present soil test results for the site, including organic matter percentage and pH, and say who carried out the sampling and when.
The applicant must explain the composting system, including bay design and how many tonnes of green waste it is expected to process each year.
The applicant must set out how seed will be saved, dried and stored over winter, naming the crops it intends to save seed from.
The applicant must describe the non-chemical methods it will use to manage insect pests and slugs on vegetable crops.
The applicant must list the tree species to be planted, the number of each, and the spacing between trees.
The applicant must provide an inventory of the hand tools and machinery to be used on site, with how each will be maintained and kept secure.
The applicant must explain how people with limited mobility, including wheelchair users, can reach and move around the growing areas, with path widths and surfaces.
The applicant must show a seasonal calendar listing the key sowing, planting and harvesting windows and the expected last spring frost date.
The applicant must explain the irrigation method for the beds and how often and at what time of day crops will be watered during dry spells.
The applicant must present a crop rotation plan that shows which plant families follow each other across the plots and over how many years.
The applicant must describe the habitat features planned for pollinators and the area, in square metres or hedge length in metres, they will cover.
The applicant must explain how weeds will be controlled without herbicides, including the mulch materials used and the depth they will be applied.
The applicant must describe the measures to prevent soil erosion and run-off on the sloping ground, naming the structures or plantings to be installed.
The applicant must describe the propagation space where seedlings will be raised, including its size and how it will be heated or ventilated.
The applicant must explain how harvested produce will be cleaned, cooled and stored after picking, including the storage conditions and holding times.
The applicant must describe how winter waterlogging will be managed, including the drains, ditches or raised areas to be built.
The applicant must explain how crops and young trees will be protected from deer, rabbits and other grazing animals, including fence type and height.
The applicant must report what the land was previously used for and how any contamination was investigated and cleared before growing food.
The applicant must describe how harvest yields will be weighed and recorded, including the units, frequency and who records them.
The applicant must explain how disagreements between members will be resolved, including who makes the final decision when mediation has failed to produce agreement.
The applicant must show how much matched funding has been secured, naming each source, the amount pledged and the date on which each contribution will be released.
The applicant must provide a budget broken down by spending category, including a contingency allowance expressed as a percentage of the total amount requested.
The applicant must describe how volunteers will be recruited, including which groups of people will be approached and which channels will be used to reach them.
The applicant must set out the training volunteers will receive before starting work, including its duration, who delivers it and how competence is confirmed.
The applicant must describe its safeguarding arrangements for children and adults at risk, including the named lead, vetting checks and the procedure for reporting concerns.
The applicant must demonstrate how the site will be usable by disabled visitors, specifying the physical adaptations planned and any alternative formats in which information will be provided.
The applicant must explain how personal data about participants will be stored, who can access it, how long it is kept and how it is deleted.
The applicant must list the measurable indicators it will use to judge success, with baseline figures, targets and the method of collecting each measure.
The applicant must state the schedule on which progress reports will be submitted to the funder, including the content of each report and who signs it off.
The applicant must identify its formal partners and describe what each contributes, with evidence that the arrangement is written down and agreed by both sides.
The applicant must confirm that public liability insurance is in place, stating the level of cover provided and the date on which the policy is next renewed.
The applicant must describe how financial and project records will be kept, how long they will be retained and who can inspect them on request.
The applicant must outline how it will keep neighbouring residents informed and involved, naming the communication channels to be used and how often updates will be given.
The applicant must set out who sits on its governing board, how many seats there are, how long terms last and how members of the board are elected or appointed.
The applicant must describe its financial controls, including who authorises payments, how many signatures are required and how bank statements are checked and reconciled.
The applicant must explain how the project will continue after the grant ends, including its future sources of income and who will take responsibility for upkeep.
The applicant must identify the main risks to delivery, rating each by likelihood and impact and naming the person responsible for managing each risk.
The applicant must explain how it will reach residents who are not usually involved in community activity, such as people who speak little English, and what support it will offer them to take part.
The applicant must explain how contractors and suppliers will be selected, including the number of quotes sought and the value above which a formal tender is used.

sections.text: Our site entrance sits at the top of a narrow farm lane, so working vehicles need careful planning. The existing field gate will be widened from three to four and a half metres and fitted with a gate that swings fully back against the hedge. Inside the gate we will lay a stone hardcore apron large enough for a delivery lorry to turn without reversing along the lane. Compost, wood chip and tree deliveries will use a marked route along the field edge to the stockpile area, which keeps heavy wheels off the beds. Drivers will be asked to call ahead so that a volunteer can open the gate and walk them in. The lane itself is a public track with passing places, and our neighbours have agreed that large deliveries will arrive only on Tuesday and Thursday mornings. A sign at the junction warns of slow vehicles, and the speed on site is limited to ten miles an hour. The haulage route is surfaced with recycled aggregate that the lane's owner has agreed to share, and we will inspect it for ruts after wet weather.

The orchard and hedge planting will introduce 180 trees in total across the lower fields. The orchard block takes 40 apple trees on semi-vigorous rootstock, 20 pears, 15 plums and 10 damsons, all set at five metres between trees and five metres between rows. Along the field edge we will plant a double staggered hedge of 60 whips: hawthorn, blackthorn, hazel and field maple, with 25 centimetres between plants and 40 between the two rows. Another 20 trees form a shelter belt of alder and birch at two metres apart, to break the prevailing wind from the west. Five walnut trees will stand singly at the corners at ten metres from any other tree, as they are large and cast heavy shade. The apple varieties have been chosen from local heritage stock, and every tree will be tagged with species and planting date. The layout has been drawn at one to five hundred scale and is included as Appendix F, with a table of each block, count and spacing, so that the final numbers can be checked against what is in the ground. A map hangs in the shed.

We collect only what we need: a participant's name, a contact number or email address and, for some activities, an emergency contact and any health needs they wish to tell us about. Paper forms are scanned within a week and then shredded; the scans are held in a password-protected folder on an encrypted cloud service with servers in the United Kingdom. Only the coordinator and the secretary can open the folder, and each has a personal login protected by a second step on their phone. Session leaders receive a printed list of emergency contacts for their group only, and must hand it back at the end of the day. Records for casual visitors are deleted after twelve months, and records for regular volunteers two years after they leave, unless the person asks us to remove them sooner. On the first of each January the secretary runs a deletion check, and a log of what was removed is kept, without the personal details. We never sell or share information with other organisations, and we do not send marketing messages without consent. Participants can ask to see, correct or erase their data at any time by writing to the secretary, who will respond within a month.

Good decisions depend on good records, so we will keep our own weather data from the first day. A small automatic station, mounted on a post at head height in the middle of the field, logs air temperature, rainfall and wind speed every hour, and a ground thermometer in a bare bed shows soil temperature at ten centimetres. The head grower downloads the figures each Monday and enters them into a spreadsheet that goes back to the start of the project. A paper rain gauge beside the shed gives a cross-check, emptied each morning by the volunteer on duty. Over time the figures will reveal how our site differs from the nearest official weather station, which lies fifteen kilometres away on higher ground. We will plot monthly totals on a chart for the open day, and share the data with the local school, whose pupils want to use it in science lessons. Any instrument failure is noted in the log so that gaps are explained. After three years, we plan to publish a short summary of what our own climate records show.

Our growing year follows the climate of the valley floor, where the last spring frost typically falls around 12 May and the first autumn frost arrives in the second week of October. In February we sow onions, leeks and early tomatoes in the heated tunnel. March is for broad beans, peas and early potatoes outdoors, with spinach and radish in the open beds. Hardy brassicas go in the nursery during April, and we plant them out in May. Once the frost date has passed, tender crops move out: courgettes, beans, squash and sweetcorn between 15 and 30 May. June is for successional lettuce, carrots and beetroot. Harvests begin with salad and radish in late April, peas and broad beans in June, and the main flush of courgettes, tomatoes and beans from July to September. Potatoes and squash are lifted in the last week of September, before the first frost, and garlic is planted in October for next year. The calendar is drawn as a wall chart in the shed with a coloured bar for each crop, and it is revised every winter from what actually happened.

A strong public image helps a small organisation to attract support, and we have given some thought to how we present ourselves. Our name, logo and colours were designed by a local graphic artist and appear on our signs, leaflets, banners, t-shirts and website. The logo shows an oak leaf set inside a circle, and the strapline reads 'Common land, common ground'. A set of brand guidelines, one page long, explains how to use the logo and which typefaces and colours to choose, so that volunteers who make posters produce a consistent look. We have also prepared a short description of the Trust, in fifty, a hundred and two hundred words, for use in press releases and funding bids. Local newspapers and the regional radio station have featured us twice, and a photographer from the county magazine spent a morning with us last June. We hope that the project will lead to further coverage, and the coordinator will take responsibility for building good relationships with local journalists. Posters for each event are drawn from the same template, and a volunteer keeps a folder of printed examples in the hall so that newcomers can see how the look works in practice. Everyone is asked to check the spelling twice before printing.

Around one in six households in the Ashcombe estate speak Polish, Urdu or Somali at home, and few have ever visited the common. We will not wait for them to find us. In the first six months the coordinator will work with the estate's community centre and two faith groups to hold taster afternoons there, so that people can meet us in a place they already trust. Invitations will be produced in four languages, written by native speakers, and delivered by hand with the help of three bilingual volunteers who have agreed to act as community ambassadors, paid an hourly rate from the budget. At events on the site we will provide interpretation by phone or in person, picture-based signs, and free transport on the community minibus from the estate. Childcare will be available for any session aimed at parents, and refreshments will be prepared to suit halal and vegetarian diets. A fund of 2,500 will cover bus tickets, kit and waived charges, so that cost is never a reason to stay away. We will count how many participants come from the estate each quarter and ask the ambassadors what is working and what is not.

Wet soil is easily damaged, so we have rules for working it. Nobody walks on a bed that is saturated, because a single pair of boots can squeeze out the air that roots need and leave a compacted layer that lasts for years. The site lead checks the ground each morning during winter by pressing a hand into the soil, and if water seeps out, the plot is declared closed on the board by the gate. On closed days, volunteers shift to indoor tasks, such as washing pots, sharpening tools or writing labels. Where work cannot wait, we lay scaffold boards across the beds to spread the weight, and barrows are wheeled only along the hardcore paths. Machines stay in the shed until the surface is firm enough to carry a footprint without leaving a mark. Heavy deliveries are rescheduled, and the walking tractor is used only when the soil crumbles rather than smears in the fingers. Every new volunteer is told the reasons for these rules as part of their induction, so that the habit becomes second nature. A laminated photograph of a compacted bed hangs in the shed as a reminder.

Our members come from many backgrounds, and the Trust has always been proud of the friendly spirit at its work days. To keep it that way, every volunteer signs a short code of conduct on joining. It asks people to arrive on time, to listen before speaking, to share tools and tea, and to treat visitors and fellow members with courtesy. Swearing, drinking on site and unkind remarks about anyone's age, background or ability are not acceptable, and the code says so plainly in everyday language. The two session leaders carry a copy of the code and are expected to remind people of it gently where needed. Newcomers are paired with an experienced member for their first three visits, which in our experience heads off most misunderstandings about how things are done. We also keep a suggestions box in the shed, emptied monthly and read aloud at the next committee meeting, so that small irritations about rotas, parking or the state of the kettle can be raised without anyone feeling singled out. Our aim is a place where people want to come back each week, and the code is written to describe that atmosphere rather than to punish anyone who falls short of it.

Funding the project has been a team effort, and we are fortunate to have so many neighbours willing to help. Over the last year we have held a summer fete, two quiz nights in the Linnet Green social club and a sponsored walk that raised money for hand tools and a new storage shed. Local shops have kindly displayed collection tins on their counters, and a number of members set up standing orders of five or ten pounds a month. In total these small acts of generosity have brought in a little over three thousand pounds, which sits in our community account and will be used for running costs. We are very grateful to everyone concerned. Looking ahead, we plan to keep fundraising throughout the grant period, partly to keep the community feeling invested and partly to build a cushion for repairs. A crowdfunding page is being prepared, and the youth group has asked to organise a bake sale each term. These activities will not be treated as part of the formal contribution to the project cost, since they are uncertain in size and timing, but they show how many people are behind the scheme and how willing they are to give their time and money.

Heavy machinery and many boots have already cut the farm track into deep ruts, and in wet weather the surface turns to slurry that is carried into the lane. We will resurface the 180-metre track with a base layer of crushed stone, a second layer of finer aggregate and a compacted top of recycled concrete fines, laid over geotextile fabric to stop the layers mixing. A slight camber in the middle lets water shed to each side, and a roadside grip every twenty metres turns it off the surface into the verge. Potholes are filled whenever they appear, using a bucket of stone and a hand rammer, and the site lead walks the track after every large storm. The gateway where vehicles turn is paved with a short concrete apron to stop the entrance from becoming a bog. We expect the work to cost far less than a full tarmac surface and to last for at least a decade with ordinary care. Heavy deliveries will be asked to avoid the track when the ground is saturated. The costs of stone and fabric are within the quote already obtained from a local haulier.

The site lies on the edge of Thornwick Vale, at the end of a lane that is shared with a small farm. There is no public bus on weekdays, but a community minibus runs twice a week from the village green to the market town of Ashcombe, and the driver has agreed to stop at the gate by request. Cyclists can lock their bikes at a rack beside the hall, and the lane is mostly flat, making it a pleasant ride for families. For those who drive, a gravel car park holds around twenty cars, and an overflow area on the verge is used on busy days. The site is open to everybody from dawn until dusk, seven days a week, and we ask only that visitors close the gate behind them and keep dogs on leads. Maps showing walking routes, a seating area and the hall are fixed to the noticeboard at the entrance, and we publish an opening times sheet on the parish website. Local people have told us how much they value the freedom to walk through on their way to the shops.

Every crate that comes off the beds is weighed before it is washed. A digital hanging scale, accurate to ten grams, is fixed to the beam at the wash station, and the harvest lead notes the weight of each crop in kilograms on a tablet, together with the date and the bed number. Entries are made at every harvest, which means up to four times a week in summer, and are never left to the end of the day. A simple spreadsheet adds up the totals by crop, bed and month. Waste is weighed separately, in the same units, so that we know how much was lost to damage or pests. On the first Monday of each month, the totals are checked against the sales sheet by a second volunteer, and any large differences are investigated. Yield per square metre is then calculated for each bed, using its measured area. At the end of the season, a one-page summary is produced and pinned in the shed, showing the best and weakest crops. A paper backup sheet hangs beside the scale in case the tablet runs out of charge or breaks.

We believe it is important to listen to the people who use the site, and to learn from them as we go. For that reason we will place a comments book in the hall and a small box for written suggestions at the entrance, and we will invite feedback at every open day. At the end of each season, the trustees will hold a review evening to which all members and neighbours are welcome. At these evenings we will ask three open questions: what has gone well, what has not, and what should we try next? The answers will be written on flip charts, photographed and typed up so that they can be shared with everyone. In the past, this process has led to practical improvements, such as moving the tea table closer to the path and changing the time of the Tuesday session from eleven to ten o'clock. The trustees take the view that talking face to face is the best way to learn, and that formal surveys can feel intrusive in a small village. We will carry on in this spirit and record every change that results from what we hear.

Many of our volunteers tell us that the social side matters as much as the work. The tea break at half past ten is a fixed point in every session, and the conversation around the shed table has led to friendships, lifts to hospital appointments and at least one marriage. We have therefore tried to protect that atmosphere as we grow. New volunteers are always introduced by name at the start of the day, and the session leader will pair them with someone who can answer questions. Jobs are offered in a range of sizes, from ten-minute tasks for people who tire easily to full-day projects for those who want a challenge. Nobody is ever required to attend on a particular day, and people may drop in whenever they like. We ask only that they sign the register for safety reasons. Our experience is that volunteers stay when they feel valued and are not pressured, and when the work they are given matches their strength and interests. We will keep these habits in place when the number of volunteers grows, and have made provision for a second kettle.

A good seedling begins with a good mix, and we have worked out a recipe based on what we can make ourselves. Our seed compost is two parts sieved leaf mould, one part garden compost, passed through a one-centimetre mesh, and one part coarse sand to keep it open and free-draining. For modules we use a finer blend, with the compost screened twice, which gives tiny roots plenty of contact. Seed is sown by hand into trays of 40 or 104 cells, depending on the crop, and covered to a depth about twice its own width. Large seeds such as beans and squash go in individually, while small seeds like lettuce and leeks are sown in a pinch of two or three. Trays are watered from below by standing them in a shallow tray, and labelled with variety and date on a wooden tag. Peas and beans are sown into old guttering sections and slid into the bed. All trays and pots are collected, scrubbed and reused. A notebook records the sowing date and the number of seedlings that emerge.

In March an independent soil advisor visited Hollowmere Field and took twenty-four cores across the four growing plots, walking a W-shaped route and sampling to fifteen centimetres. The cores were bulked into one bag per plot and sent to an agricultural laboratory, and the results came back in April. Organic matter averages 3.8 percent, rising to 5.1 on the old garden plot beside the farmhouse and dropping to 2.6 on the exposed western terrace. Soil pH runs from 6.2 to 6.9, with a mean of 6.5, which suits almost everything on our crop list without liming. Phosphorus is moderate, and potassium is low on the terrace, so we will concentrate our comfrey mulch there. Texture is a silty clay loam on three plots and a lighter sandy loam on the terrace. The full laboratory sheet is attached as Appendix C, and the advisor's field notes mark each sampling point on a site map. We will repeat the identical sampling pattern each March for as long as the project runs, so that changes can be compared like for like and any drift in acidity is caught early.

The coordinator will meet with the chair and treasurer every month to look at progress against the work plan. These meetings last about an hour and follow a simple agenda: what has been done, what is due in the next four weeks, whether anything is behind schedule and whether spending is on track. Notes are kept on a shared document, and actions are given a name and a date. If a problem emerges, such as a late delivery or a volunteer shortage, it is discussed straight away and the board is told by email within two days. Every three months the full board looks at the notes and decides whether the plan needs adjusting. We have found that this regular discipline helps us catch problems while they are still small, and that it keeps the coordinator from feeling isolated in a part-time post. A traffic light system marks each activity green, amber or red, and any amber item that remains amber for two months automatically moves onto the board's agenda for discussion. The notes also feed into the coordinator's own supervision sessions, where workload, training needs and any worries about the pace of the project are raised in a relaxed way.

Keeping the wider community informed is important to us, so we will publish our own account of progress each year in addition to anything sent to the funder. The annual summary will be a single printed sheet, delivered with the parish magazine to every household in the valley, and it will include a few photographs, a short note of thanks, and a plain summary of what we have spent. It will be presented at the March gathering, where members may ask questions and propose changes. A shorter version will go on the website and in the newsletter. We think this openness helps people trust the Trust, and it has been a tradition since our first year, when the treasurer drew up the accounts in felt tip on a large sheet of paper for display at the village fete. The practice has now grown into a modest document, but the spirit has not changed: anyone should be able to understand where the money came from and where it went, and nobody should have to ask twice to see the figures. The sheet is written by a different volunteer each year, which keeps the tone fresh and gives people a chance to practise their writing for a good cause.

Our programme of events is designed to appeal to a wide range of people, and we hope that every resident feels they have something to enjoy. During the first year we will run twelve open days, one a month, each with a different theme such as local history, wildlife spotting, craft skills or seasonal food. There will be tea and cake at every one, and activities for children and adults alike. We will also offer a monthly quiet afternoon aimed at people who find crowds tiring, with a smaller group and gentler pace. Entry to all events is free, and nobody has to book. Some events will be held jointly with other village groups, such as the Women's Institute, the history society and the knitting circle, and we hope this will bring new faces to the site. We will count the number of visitors at each event and ask them to fill in a short card saying what they liked and what they would change. The results will shape the following year's calendar, and we will publish a summary for anyone who is curious.

The vegetable area covers about 4,000 square metres and is divided into four plots of equal size, each laid out in thirty beds. Beds are 1.2 metres wide with 40-centimetre paths between them, so that every bed can be reached from either side without treading on the soil. They run north to south across the gentle slope. Plots are numbered one to four from the farmhouse side, and each bed has a small painted stake at its end with plot and bed number. A large site map at the gate shows the arrangement, and every volunteer is shown how to find their way around it. Water points sit at the head of each plot, and a compost bay is positioned at the corner of two plots so that barrowing distances are short. The plan leaves a metre-wide headland at the field edge for turning the walking tractor. Setting out the beds will be done in the first month, using string lines and a measuring tape, with a local surveyor checking the right angles and levels. Each bed is recorded on a sheet that can be updated from year to year.

The less we need to water, the better, so we will rely on practices that keep moisture in the soil. All beds are mulched with five centimetres of compost or straw after the soil has warmed, which cuts evaporation sharply. Beds run north to south so that each row shades its neighbour at midday, and tall crops like beans are placed on the western side of shorter ones. Plants are set slightly closer than usual so that leaves meet and form a living canopy. Shade cloth at thirty percent can be stretched across the lettuce hoops during heatwaves. We avoid hoeing in dry weather, as it brings damp soil to the surface where it dries out, and we pull weeds early before they compete for moisture. A windbreak of hazel hurdles at the western edge reduces drying winds. Rather than recording how much water we apply, we measure the effect, by comparing yields and survival across mulched and unmulched trial beds. Over three years we expect to see which of these practices pays back the most for the least effort.

We have walked the site with a wheelchair user, a blind resident and a member of the local deaf club, and their advice has shaped the plans. A level main path, two metres wide and surfaced in compacted fine gravel, will link the car park, the hall and the central meeting area, with a gradient never steeper than one in twenty. Two parking bays near the gate will be marked for blue badge holders, and the hall entrance will gain a ramped approach with handrails on both sides. Inside, a new accessible washroom with a drop-down rail and an emergency pull cord will be installed. Benches with arm rests will be placed every thirty metres along the path, and tactile paving will mark the edges of any steps. A hearing loop will be fitted in the hall. Information will be offered in large print, in an audio version recorded by local volunteers, and in a short captioned film, and our leaflets will use plain English with symbols. Staff and volunteers will be trained to guide visitors who are blind. We will ask the same three advisers to inspect the finished works before opening, and any shortcomings they find will be put right at our own cost.

We will not manage wildlife blindly, so we plan to find out what actually uses the farm. Four motion-triggered trail cameras will be strapped to posts at hedge gaps, the stream bank and the edge of the orchard, each fixed at knee height and left in place for fourteen days at a time. Volunteers retrieve the memory cards each fortnight and label each image by species, date and time. Early results from a trial last winter showed roe deer, foxes, badgers, a hare and a barn owl, and no sign yet of rabbits. A simple spreadsheet will tally visits, so that we learn which animals appear, how often and where they walk. Photos from the cameras will be shown at the open day, and some may be used in the school pack. Images that show people are deleted immediately, in line with the privacy sign at the gate. The aim is to appreciate and understand our neighbours, not to count them out. If a particular species becomes a problem, we will first look at where it came from before choosing any response.

Disputes are bound to arise in any group of volunteers, so the Trust has agreed a ladder in advance. A member with a grievance first raises it directly with the person concerned, ideally within a fortnight. If that goes nowhere, either side can ask the secretary to arrange a facilitated conversation led by one of two trained mediators drawn from the neighbouring parish of Ashcombe, neither of whom belongs to the Trust. Should the mediators report that no settlement can be reached after two sessions, the matter passes to the trustee board, which hears both accounts in writing and in person. The chair holds the casting vote, but only after the board has voted, and any trustee with a personal stake in the quarrel must leave the room. The board's ruling is final within the Trust and is minuted with its reasons. A member who remains unhappy may leave the Trust or approach the county voluntary sector council, but cannot reopen the same issue for twelve months. We chose this sequence because it stops small quarrels from reaching the board while guaranteeing that every dispute ends with a named body able to decide it. The ladder is printed in the members' handbook and explained to every newcomer at their induction evening.

Finished compost is only worth making if it goes on the ground at the right time and in the right amount, so we have planned its use closely. Beds that will carry heavy feeders, such as squash and leeks, receive a layer about four centimetres deep in late winter, forked in lightly at the surface. Lighter feeders get two centimetres, and the carrot bed gets none at all, since fresh richness makes roots fork. Seed compost is screened through a one-centimetre mesh and used for module trays, while rougher material goes under the fruit bushes and around the young trees. Once or twice a season we will steep a sack of compost in a barrel of water to make a liquid feed for tomatoes and peppers. Nothing is applied to frozen or waterlogged ground. The head grower keeps a chart showing which bed received compost, how much by the barrowload, and when, so that heavy applications are not repeated on the same patch two years running. Surplus compost is sieved, bagged and kept dry for use in the nursery in spring.

We will not use synthetic sprays. Instead, pests are managed through a layered set of physical and biological measures. Brassicas and carrots are covered from sowing with fine insect mesh pinned to hoops, which keeps out cabbage white butterflies, root flies and flea beetle. Slugs are the biggest threat to young plants in our damp valley, so we will water beneficial nematodes onto the beds in April and again in September, and sink beer traps along the edges of lettuce rows. Evening torch rounds in the wet weeks let volunteers collect slugs by hand and carry them to the far hedge. Strips of calendula and alyssum bring hoverflies and lacewings, whose larvae eat aphids, and a small pond near the tunnel supports frogs and toads. Aphid clusters on broad beans are pinched off at the tips, which both removes the insects and encourages pods. Sticky yellow cards in the polytunnel give early warning of whitefly. Each week the head grower walks the beds with a notebook, and a population is only acted on once it passes a threshold written on the shed wall.

Any grant we receive will be paid into a dedicated project account at our bank, separate from the Trust's general funds, so that the money can always be traced. The account requires two signatories for every withdrawal, and statements are reviewed monthly by the treasurer and presented to the trustees. We will draw on the grant in stages, matching each payment request to a completed piece of work, and we will keep the original invoices and delivery notes in a folder that the funder is welcome to inspect. Where we are asked to spend money before the grant instalment lands, the treasurer will seek the trustees' written approval and record the reason. Interest earned on balances held in the account will stay in the project rather than going into general funds. Should any money remain unspent at the end of the grant period, we will write to the funder to ask whether it may be carried forward or must be returned, and we will not commit it to anything new until we have a reply. These arrangements are modelled on how we handled a small lottery award three years ago, which the funder's officer described as tidy and easy to follow.

To find out whether our efforts make any difference, we will survey pollinators every month from April to September. Along a fixed route of fifty metres through the beds and orchard, a trained volunteer walks at a slow pace on a warm, dry day between ten and four, and counts every bee, hoverfly, butterfly and moth that lands on a flower within two metres. Species are identified from a photographic key where possible, or grouped broadly, such as bumblebees, solitary bees and hoverflies. Each walk takes fifteen minutes and is recorded on a standard sheet that goes into the national pollinator monitoring scheme. We will also place a few simple pan traps, small coloured bowls of soapy water, on two days each summer to capture insects too small to count by sight. The first year's results will form a baseline, and the second and third years will show whether numbers rise. A local naturalist society has offered to check our identifications. The data will be shown at the autumn open day in a simple chart. Each autumn a volunteer will compare the counts with the previous year and write a short plain note for everyone who helps on the site.

Safety on the site is taken seriously by everyone involved, and the trustees review it at each meeting. Before any new activity begins, a session leader walks the area with a checklist, looking for uneven ground, overhanging branches, broken glass and other hazards, and notes anything that needs attention. A weekly inspection of the paths, gates and fences is carried out on Saturday mornings, and defects are written into a log kept in the shed. Tools are checked and cleaned after every session and sharpened when needed. The hall has smoke alarms and a fire extinguisher, which are tested monthly, and a fire evacuation plan is displayed by the door. Visitors are asked to keep to marked paths and to supervise any children in their care. In the last five years, we have had no serious accidents, and no complaint has ever been made against us. We believe this good record is down to the common sense of our volunteers and the habit of reporting small concerns quickly, and we intend to maintain these routines as the project expands. The checklist was drawn up with advice from a retired health and safety officer who lives in Thornwick Vale and still visits us once a year to see how it works.

The Trust has always seen its site as a welcoming place for families, and we are keen to build on that. A weekly Saturday morning session for children aged six to twelve has run for two years, led by a member who is a retired primary school teacher. The children plant seeds, build bug hotels and make labels, and parents are asked to stay and take part. Numbers have grown from six to twenty-three, and the group now has its own corner of the site with a low fence and a small gate. Several parents have become regular volunteers, and the group has received warm thanks in the school newsletter. We also host two visits a year from the Pennybrook infant school, with a teacher and helpers accompanying each class. The activities are fun and seasonal, and we make sure there is always something for children who prefer to watch or draw. We would like to expand the programme to the school holidays, and have included a modest sum in the budget for craft materials and refreshments, along with the cost of a second leader to keep the groups at a manageable size.

The board of trustees meets every second Tuesday of the month in the hall, with an agenda circulated a week beforehand. A quorum of five is required for any decision to be valid, and most business is dealt with by general agreement. Where a vote is needed, a simple majority of those present carries the motion, and the chair has a second, casting vote if the numbers are equal. Items on each agenda include an update from the coordinator, the financial position, any correspondence and reports from the working groups. The secretary records decisions and who is to carry them out, and the minutes are circulated within a week. Any trustee may ask to add an item to the agenda by contacting the secretary at least three days before the meeting. Meetings last about two hours and finish with a short period in which any member of the public present may ask a question. We usually have two or three members in attendance. The trustees feel that the monthly meeting pattern is manageable for people who also hold full-time jobs.

Alongside the main project, we will need to take care of the equipment and buildings that the grant will help us to buy. Tools, mowers and other machinery will be stored in a locked steel container beside the hall, which is bolted to a concrete base and fitted with a closed shackle padlock. A marking pen is used to put the Trust's postcode on each item, and an inventory is kept by the coordinator, who checks it every month. Keys to the container are held by five named people and logged in a book. We have installed a simple alarm in the hall and keep valuable items out of sight overnight. The hall itself is a stone building of considerable age, and we have a maintenance plan which includes checking the roof and gutters each autumn, servicing the boiler each year and testing the electrics every five years. Repairs costing less than 500 may be authorised by the treasurer, and anything larger is brought to the board. We hope that careful stewardship will let the building and its contents last for many decades.

The coordinator will be employed by the Trust on a permanent part-time contract, and we have taken advice about how best to recruit. The post will be advertised for four weeks in the parish magazine, on the county voluntary sector jobs website and on the noticeboards in Ashcombe. Applicants will be asked to supply a short letter and a CV, and a panel of three trustees will interview the shortlisted candidates. We will be looking for experience of working with volunteers and communities, good organisation and a friendly manner. The salary has been set at a level comparable with similar posts in the county, with a pension contribution and twenty-five days of holiday, and an employment adviser has checked the contract. The postholder will be supervised monthly by the chair and will have an annual appraisal. We expect the appointment to be made within eight weeks of the grant being confirmed, and a trustee has volunteered to act as interim coordinator if there is any delay. The adviser also recommended that we keep a short job description on file and review it every two years so that it remains accurate. Once the postholder is in place, we will arrange a two-week induction, including introductions to partners, neighbours and the main volunteers.

The treasurer's role is central to the Trust, and we have been fortunate to have the same person for the last four years. She is a qualified bookkeeper, and she brings a calm and careful approach to the work. At each trustee meeting she presents a simple report showing money received, money paid out and the bank balance. The report is checked by the chair before the meeting and is discussed openly. She also prepares the annual accounts, which are presented to members in March and filed with the charity regulator within the deadline. When the treasurer is away, her deputy steps in and uses a handover checklist that sets out each task and where to find the relevant papers. We have started to train a second person in the accounting software, so that knowledge is not held by one individual. Members have commented that they appreciate the way the finances are explained without jargon. We think it is important that the position carries respect, and we have given the treasurer a small honorarium to thank her for the time she gives.

No single person can move the Trust's money. Every payment from the bank account needs two of the four named signatories, who are the chair, the treasurer and two other trustees, and no signatory may sign a cheque or approve an online transfer made out to themselves or a relative. Online banking is set up with a maker and checker arrangement: the treasurer prepares a payment and a second signatory approves it from a separate device. Payments above 1,000 must also have been approved in advance by the board and noted in the minutes. Each month, a trustee who is not a signatory receives the bank statement directly from the bank, compares it line by line with the treasurer's ledger, and signs and dates the reconciliation. Petty cash is limited to 150, kept in a locked tin, and counted every quarter by two people. The books are examined each year by an independent examiner who has no connection with the Trust, and her letter is presented to the members. We have set out these steps in a financial procedures document, which was adopted by the board in January and is reviewed annually.

Raising enough money to cover running costs after the grant ends is a challenge, and we have thought hard about it. Our plan is to build a mixture of small income streams so that we are not dependent on any one source. These include hire of the hall for private events, which should bring in about four thousand pounds a year, a plant sale each spring, a friends scheme with an annual subscription of twenty pounds, and a modest charge for school visits. We also intend to apply to local trusts for small grants for specific items. We have prepared a draft income plan that shows how these streams could build up over three years, and it suggests that we could cover about seventy per cent of our running costs by the end of the funding period. The trustees recognise that the figures are estimates and plan to revisit them every six months. If income grows more slowly than hoped, we have agreed to reduce opening hours rather than cut the quality of what we offer. The trustees would rather grow carefully than depend on a promise of money that may not arrive.

Rotation is not our only tool for keeping the soil busy. Within each season we practise intercropping, which means growing two crops in the same bed so that they use space and light at different times. Fast radishes are sown between slow parsnip rows and are harvested long before the parsnips need the room. Lettuce grows in the shade of tall tomatoes in midsummer, and nasturtiums trail beneath the squash to draw blackfly away. Where a bed is cleared in early August, we sow a green manure of phacelia or field beans, which holds nutrients over winter, protects the surface from heavy rain and is dug in the following spring. Winter rye is sown after potatoes and cut down before it sets seed. These combinations were chosen from trials on neighbouring market gardens and from the experience of our head grower. We will note in the planting diary which pairings give the best yield per square metre, and drop any that crowd each other. The aim is to keep roots in the ground and leaves above it for as many months as possible.

The grant pays for building and start-up, not for running the place forever, so we have planned for the years that follow. By the end of year three, we expect to cover our annual running costs of about 38,000 from four sources: hall hire and a small cafe, which we project at 14,000; a social prescribing contract with the Pennybrook Health Centre, worth 9,000; school visit fees at 6,000; and 9,000 from a friends scheme and local donations. In the meantime, we will build a reserve of three months' costs by saving ten per cent of earned income from the first year. Responsibility for upkeep will pass to a land stewardship committee of volunteers, chaired by a trustee, which will keep a rolling five year maintenance schedule. The part-time coordinator post will continue if income allows; if not, the trustees will fall back on a volunteer coordinator supported by a small expenses budget. Under the lease, the parish council remains the freeholder and will step in on any structural matters. We will revisit this plan at each annual meeting and tell the funder if our forecasts change materially.

Privacy matters to the members of our Trust, and we have decided to be open about what we do. A short statement is printed on the back of our membership form, explaining that we use names and contact details to send notices of meetings and invitations to events. The same statement is displayed in the hall and published on the website. Members are asked to tick a box to say whether they are happy to receive email, post or telephone calls, and they can change their minds whenever they like by telling the secretary. We take photographs at events, and a notice at the entrance explains that anyone who does not wish to appear in them should tell a leader, who will make sure they are left out. Photographs of children are only taken with a parent's written consent. We have not had any complaints about our approach so far, and we believe the straightforward language we use helps people feel comfortable. The parish clerk has kindly offered to look over our wording once a year to check that it remains understandable.

Compost made carelessly can spread weeds and disease, so we manage heat as well as volume. Each bay carries a long-stemmed thermometer, and the site lead records the temperature at the centre of every heap twice a week. Our rule is that a heap must reach at least 55 degrees Celsius and hold it for three days before it is turned, because that is enough to kill most weed seeds and plant pathogens. If a heap stays cool, we add nitrogen-rich material such as fresh grass clippings, or damp it down; if it overheats, we turn it early to let air in. Diseased tomato foliage, bindweed roots and anything flowering with ripe seed go into a separate sealed drum and are rotted for a full year before use. A simple cress germination test on each finished batch confirms that the compost is mature and not harmful to seedlings. We do not accept meat, dairy or cooked food, and a laminated sign explains this by the bays. Any compost that fails the cress test is returned to the heap rather than used on the beds.

Our trustees come from a range of backgrounds and bring many useful skills. The present chair is a retired surveyor who lives in Thornwick Vale and has overseen several building projects, and the treasurer is a bookkeeper who works part-time for a firm in Ashcombe. The secretary is a former secondary school teacher, and two other trustees have experience in nursing and social work. A young farmer represents the agricultural community, and a student at the further education college joined last year. New trustees receive a short induction pack explaining their legal duties as charity trustees, covering topics such as acting in the Trust's interests, avoiding conflicts of interest and making sure that the Trust spends its money properly. Each trustee is also invited to attend a one-day course run by the county voluntary sector council. We believe that the combination of local knowledge and professional skills serves the Trust well, and we are glad to have a mix of ages. Trustees are not paid, though reasonable travel costs and the fee for any approved course are refunded on request. We have never had difficulty filling vacancies, and two of our newer trustees first came to the Trust as volunteers.

Three organisations have agreed to work with us, and each relationship is set down in a signed memorandum of understanding, copies of which are enclosed. Ashcombe High School will send a class of around thirty pupils for half a day each fortnight in term time, provide a teacher to accompany them and give the Trust access to its minibus for occasional trips. The Pennybrook Health Centre will refer patients to a social prescribing programme on our site, with a link worker attending the first visit of each referred person, and will give us a short report each year on how many people were referred. Marlowe Reach Parish Council owns the freehold of the land and has granted us a twenty-five year lease at a peppercorn rent, with a clause allowing it to terminate only after a year's notice and a hearing. Each memorandum names a contact on both sides, sets out what is expected, and will be reviewed every twelve months at a joint meeting. They were signed by the head teacher, the practice manager and the clerk to the council, and by our chair, in the presence of a witness, last month. We have also drawn up a list of informal supporters, who are not listed here.

Our kit is deliberately modest. The hand tools are eight spades, eight digging forks, six hoes of different patterns, ten trowels, four wheelbarrows, six pairs of loppers and secateurs, two billhooks and a pair of long-handled shears. Machinery is limited to a two-wheel walking tractor with a rotavator and a ridging attachment, a petrol strimmer, a battery hedge trimmer, and a small electric chipper for shredding prunings. Everything is cleaned with a stiff brush after use and wiped with an oily rag; blades are sharpened by the site lead each Friday, and the tractor is serviced once a year by a local mechanic, who also checks the guards. Each item carries a painted coloured band so we can see at a glance what belongs to the project. Tools live in the locked steel container beside the barn, each on a labelled hook with a painted outline, and the machines are chained to a ground anchor inside it. A sign-out sheet records who took what and when. Any missing item is reported to the site lead the same day. A short repair list is reviewed each winter, and worn items are replaced.

We want every bed to be reachable by someone who cannot bend or walk far. The main paths through the growing area will be one and a half metres wide, enough for two wheelchairs to pass, and will be laid with compacted limestone dust over a geotextile sheet, a firm and slightly textured surface that drains well and does not turn to mud. Gradients along the route never exceed one in twenty, with level resting spots every thirty metres. Side paths between beds are one metre wide and surfaced with the same material. Two sections of raised bed, 75 centimetres high and 90 centimetres across, have an open space beneath for a wheelchair user's knees, and one long bench-height tunnel table serves the propagation work. Edges of paths carry a low timber kerb so that wheels and sticks do not slip into the beds. Tap points sit at hip height with lever handles. A hard-standing parking bay for two vehicles lies at the gate, joined to the path by a dropped kerb. The route will be walked and tested with a local mobility group before opening.

Seed saving begins in the plot, long before harvest. We will keep seed from climbing beans, peas, lettuce, tomatoes, calendula and a local pumpkin that has been grown in the valley for generations. Beans and peas are left on the vine until the pods rattle, then picked on a dry afternoon and spread on mesh trays in the potting shed. Lettuce is cut as a whole stalk and shaken into a paper bag. Tomato seed is fermented in water for three days, washed clean and dried on a plate. Everything dries in a ventilated loft for two to three weeks, until a bean snaps rather than bends. We then pack it into glass jars with a sachet of dry silica or rice, label it with variety, year and plot, and keep the jars in the cool north cellar at around eight degrees. A small paper envelope of each batch goes in a tin as a backup. Before sowing each spring, we test germination on damp kitchen paper, and discard any seed that sprouts below seventy percent. Saved lots are rotated so the oldest seed is always used first.

Laboratory figures only tell part of the story, so we also read our ground by hand and eye. Each plot is assessed with a spade test: a block of soil about the size of a shoe box is lifted, dropped from knee height and broken apart so that we can judge crumb size, root depth and any smearing or compacted layers. We score each plot from one to five and photograph the profile against a ruler. Earthworm counts are taken in a quarter-metre pit in October and again in April, and a simple ring infiltration test shows how quickly a downpour soaks in. The old garden plot has dark, open, crumbly ground with plenty of worms, while the western terrace is pale, tight and puddles after rain. Volunteers who join the soil walk learn to recognise these differences, and the scores go on a shared sheet in the shed. We will repeat the visual assessment every autumn so the whole team can see whether the beds are loosening up. It costs almost nothing and gives us a living picture of how the soil responds to mulch, digging and traffic.

Most of our first-year seed will be bought, because growing a reliable crop in the first season matters more than self-sufficiency. We will order from two regional suppliers known for open-pollinated and organic varieties, placing the order in early January to get the full range before popular lines run out. Each packet is checked on arrival for the sow-by date and stored unopened in a biscuit tin in the cool cellar until needed. The head grower will draw up a sowing list from the plot map, working out how many metres of row each crop needs so that we do not waste packets. Small leftovers are resealed with a clip and used within a year. We prefer varieties bred for cooler, damper conditions, such as slow-bolting spinach and blight-tolerant potatoes. Suppliers will also be asked to confirm that seed is untreated and not coated with fungicide. Any unused packets at the end of the season are logged and, if still viable, offered to the nursery group for their own trays, so nothing is simply thrown away. Receipts and batch numbers are filed in a folder so any problem seed can be traced back to its supplier quickly.

Welcoming visitors is something that the Trust takes seriously, and we have tried to make the experience a pleasant one. A small team of greeters, wearing bright green aprons, stands at the gate during every open day, offering a smile, a leaflet and a cup of tea. They are asked to talk to people who seem unsure, to point out the toilets and the seating, and to explain what is going on. Signs at the entrance say 'Everyone welcome' and show a simple map of the site. Our website is clear and bright, and we answer messages sent through social media within a day. Visitors' books show that people come from as far afield as the next county, and we have been pleased by comments such as 'friendly' and 'peaceful'. We think that first impressions matter and that a warm greeting makes all the difference to someone who is nervous about joining in. We intend to keep a team of greeters in place during the grant period and to offer them a short course on welcoming visitors. Greeters also carry a card with the names of the session leaders so that visitors know whom to ask for help.

At the heart of our project is a simple idea: that an area of land in the middle of the village can once again become a shared place. The common was used for generations as a meeting place, and as grazing and a short cut to the church, but over the last forty years it was gradually neglected and became overgrown. Many older residents remember it fondly, and some have told us stories of fairs, football matches and picnics that took place there. Our aim is to restore not only the physical area but also the sense that it belongs to everyone. By opening the paths, creating a welcoming meeting space and offering activities for all ages, we hope to make the common a place that people choose to visit and feel proud of. We believe that the project will leave a lasting mark on Thornwick Vale, and that our children and grandchildren will be able to enjoy what we have created. The three years of grant funding give us the chance to make this vision real. Older members have promised to record their memories of the common so that they will not be lost.

The people who live beside the site will hear about our plans before anyone else. Before work begins, the coordinator will deliver a printed letter to each of the eighty or so households within five hundred metres, giving a named telephone number and an email address for questions. Once work starts, a fortnightly note will be posted through the same doors, describing what is happening, what noise or disruption to expect and when it will finish. A monthly drop-in hour, held in the hall on the first Saturday, will let anyone raise worries face to face over a cup of tea. We will also post to the village Facebook group each week, update the parish website monthly and place a notice on the board at the lane end. Residents will be invited to join an advisory panel of six neighbours, which meets quarterly and can ask the trustees to change how work is done. Where something goes wrong, such as an unexpected delay or a burst water main, the coordinator will phone affected neighbours within twenty four hours. At the end of each year we will hold an open evening to report on progress and listen to what people think.

We want everyone in the valley to feel that the site belongs to them, and so we try to involve people in decisions about how it looks and feels. For example, last spring we held a naming competition for the new central meeting area, which attracted forty-one entries from children and adults, and the winning name was chosen by a public vote at the fete. Residents also helped to decide where to put the benches, by placing coloured stickers on a large map in the hall. Several people said they were pleased to have been asked, and some who had not previously taken part in anything we did have since become regular volunteers. In future, we plan to hold similar consultations on the design of the entrance, the choice of signs and the programme for the school holidays. Results are written up and displayed in the hall, with an explanation of which ideas were adopted and why others were not. We think this approach strengthens trust, and we will continue to use it throughout the project. Several of the best ideas, such as the ramp handrails and the planting of a memorial hedge, came from these simple exercises rather than from any formal meeting.

A good tool is only safe in trained hands, so all volunteers will receive a short induction before they use anything sharper than a trowel. The site lead demonstrates the correct way to carry, pass and put down a spade, fork or billhook, and explains why blades always face down and away from the body. Strimmers, the chipper and the walking tractor are restricted to people who have completed a half-day course with a certified instructor and signed off a practical check. Sturdy footwear is compulsory in the growing area, gloves are provided for pruning and thorny work, and ear protection and visors are worn with any engine. Younger helpers work only with child-sized hand tools under supervision. A laminated card in the shed lists the basic rules in plain words with drawings, and a first aid box with eyewash hangs by the door. Anyone who feels unwell, hurried or distracted is encouraged to stop, and no one is ever asked to operate machinery alone. We will refresh the training at the start of each season and add it to the induction record.

Pollinators will have three dedicated habitats on the site. First, a wildflower strip six metres wide and one hundred metres long, so 600 square metres, will run along the southern edge, sown with a native meadow mix of knapweed, bird's-foot trefoil, red clover and oxeye daisy. Second, we will plant 220 metres of mixed native hedge on the western and northern boundaries, including blackthorn and hawthorn for early blossom and ivy for late autumn nectar. Third, a south-facing bee bank of sandy soil, twelve metres long and one metre high, offers nesting places to solitary bees, and bundles of hollow stems hang from the barn wall for cavity nesters. A further 80 square metres of the orchard floor will be left unmown until August to protect ground-nesting bumblebees. The strip is cut once in September and the cuttings are removed, which keeps fertility low and flowers plentiful. Together these features cover roughly 1,100 square metres of the site, about a tenth of the whole, and each is marked on the habitat map attached as Appendix G. The strip will be fenced from footfall so that flowers are left undisturbed.

Anything we put on food plants has to be safe, so we plan to test the water we draw. The site has an old hand-dug well beside the orchard gate and a stream along the lower boundary, and neither has been assessed in living memory. Before the first sowing we will send samples from both to an accredited laboratory for bacteria, nitrate and heavy metals, and again at midsummer when concentrations are usually worst. The stream sample will be taken upstream of the field drain, so we know what arrives before we add anything ourselves. Results will be pinned to the gate board in plain language with a green, amber or red label. If the well fails, we will cap it for non-edible use only; if the stream shows faecal contamination, we will keep it off leafy crops and use mains water on salads instead. Hands and tools are washed at a tap with a foot pedal, and all hoses are drained and coiled off the ground after use to stop stagnant water breeding bacteria. A short clean-water protocol is pinned in the shed, and every volunteer is walked through it on their first day on site.

All paid staff and every volunteer who handles money or keys must be properly screened before they begin. For this reason, we ask each applicant to complete a short form with their name, address and two references, at least one of whom is not a relative or friend. The coordinator or secretary contacts the referees by telephone and keeps brief notes of the conversation. We do not make assumptions based on age, appearance or background, and we welcome people who may have had difficult experiences, provided they can demonstrate reliability in the role. Those who will hold keys to the hall or have access to the bank account also sign a declaration that they have no unspent convictions for dishonesty. Trustees complete a declaration of interests annually, and we keep these in a locked cabinet in the secretary's home. In six years we have turned down only one applicant for a keyholder role, and the decision was recorded, explained to the person kindly and reviewed by the chair. We think the procedure is proportionate for a small organisation, and we will apply it to new recruits equally.

Photographs and stories are among the most valuable things we gather, and we plan to keep them carefully. The project will produce a visual history of the common, with before and after pictures of every major piece of work, oral histories recorded with older residents, and a scrapbook of newspaper cuttings and event posters. A volunteer with experience of archive work has offered to organise the collection, and the county record office has advised us on how to label and store each item so that it lasts. Digital images will be saved in an open file format with a short description, and prints will be kept in acid-free sleeves in a box in the hall. We would like to share this material widely, and plan to produce a small exhibition at the end of each year and an online gallery on our website. The material will also be offered to the county record office when the project is complete, so that future researchers can see how the community brought the land back to life. Volunteers and older residents are welcome to help with scanning and cataloguing, and the work has proved a good way to bring people together on wet days.

Weeds will be held back by smothering and by timely hand work, never by chemicals. New ground is cleared by laying overlapping sheets of plain cardboard, with all tape and staples removed, directly over the grass, and covering them with ten centimetres of coarse wood chip. This blocks light for about six months, long enough to kill most perennials, and the cardboard rots into the soil afterwards. Established vegetable beds get a lighter mulch of five centimetres of finished compost, applied after planting and topped up each spring. Paths between beds are covered with fifteen centimetres of chip, which stays thick enough to resist grass. Between mulch rounds, a stirrup hoe is run lightly through the surface on dry mornings every two weeks, so small weed seedlings are cut before they root. Any weed that reaches flowering is cut and bagged to stop seeds spreading. Perennial roots such as dock and bindweed are dug out with a fork and not composted. We expect weed pressure to fall sharply by the second season, with hoeing needed less often as the mulch layer thickens and the seed bank runs down.

No volunteer will use a power tool or work alone until they have completed our induction. It runs for one three-hour evening and one four-hour Saturday morning, usually within the first month of joining. The evening covers site rules, manual handling, first aid basics and the use of protective clothing, and is delivered by the coordinator together with a qualified first aider from the Ashcombe branch of a national ambulance charity. The Saturday session is practical: a trained instructor from the county skills college demonstrates the safe use of hand tools, strimmers and wheelbarrows, and each trainee then works through a short circuit while being observed. The instructor signs a competence card for every tool the trainee has shown they can handle safely, and the card is kept in the site office. Anyone who is not yet confident simply repeats the circuit at the next session, and nobody is turned away. Refresher sessions take place every two years, and the cards are checked at the start of each season, when anything out of date is flagged to the coordinator. About thirty volunteers will take the induction in the first year, in three cohorts of ten, and the cost of instructor time is included in the budget.

Water for the growing beds will come mostly from the roofs we already have. The long barn and the potting shed together catch enough runoff to fill a bank of six linked tanks, each holding 1,000 litres, plus a lined reservoir of about 12,000 litres sunk behind the compost bays. That gives us roughly 18,000 litres in hand before the dry weeks begin. The tanks stand on a levelled gravel pad and are joined at the base with wide pipes, so they fill and empty as one body. First-flush diverters sit upstream of each gutter, and the reservoir has a floating cover to cut evaporation and keep sunlight off the water. We chose this size after working out that the beds draw about 700 litres on a hot day, which means a full store carries the site for around three weeks without mains help. If the roofs deliver more than we can hold, an overflow pipe sends the surplus into the swale along the lower hedge. Volunteers will read a simple dipstick gauge on each tank every Friday and chalk the level on a board by the gate, so everyone can see how much is left.

Many of our visitors will arrive without a car, so we have considered how people get to the site as well as what they find there. The nearest bus stop is a ten-minute walk from the lane end, on a route that runs hourly on weekdays and every two hours on Saturdays. We will post the timetable at the stop and on a board by the gate, and a volunteer will meet any group arriving by public transport. A covered rack for twelve bicycles will stand by the entrance, with room for cargo bikes. For visitors driving, a small car park at the roadside holds eight vehicles and keeps traffic out of the lane. A wayfinding sign, in large print with simple symbols, shows the walk from the bus stop and notes how long it takes. We will also publish a short map on the project's web page, with the route marked, and a phone number to call if someone gets lost. There is a bench halfway along the walk from the bus stop where anyone can sit and rest on the way.

The largest single cost in our project is the community hall refit, and we have taken care to price it properly. Three builders were asked to quote against the same written specification, which covers new insulation, a replacement boiler, a step-free entrance and an accessible washroom. The quotes arrived within eleven per cent of one another, and we chose the middle one because the firm is based in Ashcombe, has worked on listed village buildings and offered a clear programme of works. The architect who drew up the specification has agreed to inspect progress at three stages and sign off the final account. Work will be scheduled for the quiet months of January to March so that the hall can stay open for the Tuesday lunch club until the building phase begins. The builder will give a twelve month defects guarantee and will return to deal with any snagging in the first spring. We have also asked for the cost of the entrance ramp to be shown separately in the contract, because we believe other parish halls may want to see what such a feature costs in practice.

Frost is the greatest risk to our early crops, so we have prepared a series of protective measures that can be used at short notice. Horticultural fleece in two weights is stored beside the tunnel, and low hoops are kept ready to cover sown beds within ten minutes. Potatoes that have emerged are earthed up with soil when frost is forecast, and tender seedlings in the tunnel are given a second layer of fleece and a bucket of warm water placed among the trays overnight. Cloches protect individual plants such as courgettes for the first fortnight after planting out. We have placed hardy crops on the colder, lower plots and kept tender ones on the sheltered terrace, where cold air drains away. A volunteer rota assigns someone to check the evening forecast from March until the end of May and send a message to the group if the temperature is predicted to fall below two degrees. Covers go on at dusk and come off by mid-morning. A frost pocket near the stream has been identified, and we will plant it with fruit bushes rather than annual vegetables.

Beekeeping is a small but visible part of our plans. Two hives of honey bees will stand at the sheltered east end of the orchard, facing south-east so that the first sunshine warms the entrance. The hives will be managed by an experienced local beekeeper who has kept bees in the valley for twenty years and has agreed to mentor two volunteers through their first season. Inspections are made every seven to ten days between April and August, checking for queen cells, disease and stores. We will treat varroa mites with an approved organic acid only when counts pass the national threshold, and keep a written record of every visit. A small amount of honey, perhaps twenty kilograms a year, will be extracted in the barn and shared among volunteers. The hives are fenced off from the beds with a low hurdle so that bees fly up above head height. Neighbours have been told in advance, and a warning sign explains what to do if someone is stung. We recognise that honey bees do not replace wild pollinators, and the hives will be limited to two.

Our programme will include activities designed for particular age groups, so that no one feels left out. For children under five and their carers, there will be a monthly stay and play session on the hall lawn, with simple crafts, songs and storytelling. A junior club for children aged eight to twelve will meet in the school holidays, while a youth group for teenagers will run on Friday evenings during the summer. Adults of working age will be offered evening and weekend work days, and a social evening once a quarter. For older residents, we will continue the weekly tea and chat morning, and add a monthly walk at a gentle pace with regular stops. We will also hold two intergenerational days a year, where children and older people take part in activities side by side. The timetable has been shaped by conversations at public events, and we will review it each year. All sessions are free, and the coordinator will check that the programme remains balanced between age groups. The Trust has found that older people in particular appreciate a clear start time and a place to sit down at the end.

We need around forty regular volunteers by the end of the first year, and we have set out to find them in places where people already gather. Retired residents of Thornwick Vale are the group we know best, so we will give short talks at the over-sixties lunch club and the library coffee morning. We also want younger people, so the coordinator will visit the sixth form at Ashcombe High and the apprenticeship classes at the further education college, offering volunteering hours that count towards their award schemes. Parents will be reached through the primary school newsletter and the Saturday football club, and newly arrived households will receive a welcome card from the parish office with our contact details. On the practical side, a recruitment poster will go up in the post office, the surgery and both pubs, and we will post to the three village Facebook groups and the parish email list. Every request will say plainly how many hours are needed, what the tasks are and that nobody needs previous experience. We will keep a simple record of how each new volunteer heard about us, and review it after six months so that we can put more effort into the channels that actually work.

Alongside the harvest figures, we keep a careful notebook of what is happening in the beds. Once a week, the head grower walks every plot with a clipboard and records the growth stage of each crop, any signs of pests, disease or nutrient shortage, weather damage and weed pressure. Each observation is given a short code and a score from one to five, and photographs are taken of anything unusual. Notes are tidied on Friday afternoon, entered into a shared file and tagged with the bed number. Patterns emerge over the months: for instance, the repeated appearance of leaf yellowing on the western plot pointed us toward a nitrogen shortage. Volunteers are invited to add their own observations on a whiteboard in the shed, which the grower copies into the file. At the end of the year, the journal is reviewed in a meeting, and lessons are written up for the next season. The journal does not record what was harvested, which is handled elsewhere, but it explains why a crop did well or poorly and what we might do differently.

Thornwick Vale Common Land Trust is a membership organisation, and every adult living in the parish may join for a nominal annual fee. Members meet four times a year in the village hall, with the main gathering held each March, when the accounts are presented and the next twelve months of activity are agreed. Each member holds one vote, whether they joined last week or twenty years ago, and proposals pass by simple majority of those present. Notice of every meeting, together with the agenda and any papers, is posted on the hall noticeboard and sent by email at least fourteen days beforehand. Members who cannot attend may nominate another member to vote on their behalf, provided the nomination is handed to the secretary in writing. Between meetings, day to day matters are handled by working groups, each led by a convenor who reports at the next gathering. Minutes are circulated within ten days and approved at the following meeting. We have found that this steady rhythm keeps people informed and gives everyone a regular chance to speak, and we intend to hold the same pattern throughout the grant period, adding one extra evening session in the first autumn to plan the opening season.
