Our project has several aims, and we think it helps to be clear about each one. The first is to bring a neglected area of common land back into use and to open it to all residents free of charge. The second is to build a stronger sense of community in Thornwick Vale, particularly among people who live alone or have recently moved here. The third is to offer young people a place where they can learn new skills and gain confidence, and the fourth is to create a lasting organisation which can continue after the grant has ended. We see these aims as connected, since a busy, welcoming site will naturally bring people together, and an active group of volunteers will be better placed to sustain it. We have discussed the aims at three public meetings, and the version printed here reflects the changes that residents suggested. The wording was approved unanimously at the March gathering, and we will display it in the hall so that visitors can see what we are trying to achieve. Each aim has a named trustee who keeps an eye on it and reports briefly at board meetings, so that none is forgotten once the busy season begins.

Our approach to money is cautious, and we would like the funder to see how decisions about spending are made. At the start of each financial year the treasurer prepares a draft budget based on the work plan and last year's actual figures. The trustees discuss it at their January meeting, adjust it where they feel priorities have changed and then present it to the members in March for approval. Throughout the year the treasurer produces a one-page summary showing income received, money spent and the balance, which is posted on the noticeboard and discussed at each quarterly meeting. Any spending above two hundred pounds that was not in the approved budget must be agreed by the trustees in advance. We have run to a plan like this for six years, and the accounts have never shown a deficit. The members value being able to see where the money goes, and several have said that the one-page summary is the first financial document they have ever fully understood. We will continue to use the same process throughout the grant, adding a separate section for grant income and spending so that it can be read on its own.

We have adopted a written purchasing policy so that every pound is spent on a fair basis. For anything costing less than 500, the treasurer may buy from a supplier of her choice, provided the price looks reasonable. Between 500 and 5,000, we must obtain at least three written quotes against the same description of the job, and the board chooses on value for money rather than lowest price alone, recording its reasons in the minutes. Above 5,000, a formal tender is required: the coordinator and a trustee prepare a specification, advertise it on the county procurement portal and in the parish magazine for at least three weeks, and a panel of three, none of whom may have a personal link to any bidder, scores the replies against published criteria for price, quality, local benefit and experience. Trustees must declare any interest in a bidder and leave the room during the decision. Preference is given to firms in the valley where they match on quality, but this will not override the scoring. The hall refit and the main path will both go to tender, and the whole file for each purchase will be kept for inspection.

Our fertility plan sets out where we want the soil to end up, and how we intend to get there. The long-term aim is to hold pH between 6.0 and 7.0 and to lift organic matter above 4 percent on every plot, which is a level associated with good water holding and steady nutrient supply. We will not bring in bagged fertiliser. Instead, each bed receives two centimetres of finished compost every winter, green manures are sown after every early crop, and nitrogen-fixing clover is undersown beneath the brassicas. If the soil becomes too acid we will apply ground limestone at no more than two hundred grams per square metre in a single dressing, and never in the same season as manure. Wood ash from the tool-shed stove, in small amounts, can top up potassium. Records of everything added will be kept in a field notebook by the head grower, with date, material and weight. We expect the first visible gains in the second growing season, and we will review the amounts annually with an experienced adviser before changing anything. Compost amounts are weighed rather than guessed.

Staying in touch with people who have shown an interest in the project is a priority, and we are building a simple mailing list to do so. Anyone can sign up at the hall, on the website or at one of our open days, and we will send a monthly email with news, photographs and an invitation to the next work day. We use a free newsletter service that lets people unsubscribe with one click, and we aim to keep each message short and cheerful. We expect the list to grow from about 150 addresses now to around 600 by the end of the first year, mostly through events and word of mouth. Open rates are checked after every mailing so that we can see which topics people enjoy, and a quarterly printed sheet is also produced for residents who do not use email. Volunteers who help to compile the newsletter meet in the hall on the first Wednesday of the month, and the group is always looking for another person who enjoys writing short, friendly pieces about what is going on.

The Trust was formed seven years ago by a small group of neighbours who were concerned about the state of the common. At first there were just eleven of us, meeting in a kitchen. We registered as a charitable incorporated organisation in the second year, and have grown steadily since, to 212 members today. In that time we have cleared the main path, restored the old stone gateposts, repaired the hall roof and held more than sixty public events. We have a record of delivering what we promise, and have managed three small grants totalling about 28,000 without any queries from the funders. Our work has been praised by the parish council and by visitors from other villages. This application is our first for a major grant, and it represents a significant step. We have chosen to go for a larger project because the community has shown so much enthusiasm and because we believe the land can be of real benefit to people of all ages and backgrounds. The trustees are confident that we have the experience to do it.

The Trust holds a public liability policy with a specialist insurer of voluntary organisations, and a certificate is attached. It provides cover of up to five million pounds for any one claim, and includes volunteers and members of the public who use the site, as well as events held in the hall. The current policy runs until the thirtieth of June, and the treasurer has entered the renewal date in the shared diary with a reminder set eight weeks beforehand, so that quotations can be compared and the board can approve the payment in good time. The annual premium is about 640, and a line for it has been included in the running costs of the budget. Employers' liability cover of ten million pounds will be added from the day the coordinator is appointed, as the law requires, and we have asked the insurer to confirm that our planned activities, including the use of strimmers by trained volunteers, fall within the terms. If our activities change, we will tell the insurer before they begin. A copy of the certificate is displayed in the hall, and a further copy has been given to the parish council, as a condition of the lease.

Alongside the sum requested here, we have already lined up 42,500 in additional money, which is just over a third of the full project cost. The largest piece, 20,000, comes from the Marlowe Reach Parish Council, whose members voted it through in September; it will arrive in two equal instalments on the first of April and the first of October next year. A further 12,000 has been pledged by the Pennybrook Cooperative Bank from its community dividend fund, payable in a single transfer on the fifteenth of May. The Harrowgate Fold Allotment Society will contribute 6,500 from its reserves, drawn down in July, and the remaining 4,000 is the cash value of a legacy left to the Trust and already sitting in our deposit account. Letters confirming each of the first three pledges are attached to this application, and the bank statement showing the legacy is included as supporting evidence. We have not counted volunteer time or donated materials towards this total, though both will be considerable. If any pledged sum arrived late, the legacy balance could bridge the gap for up to eight weeks, so the work programme would not stall while we waited. We will tell the funder immediately should any contribution change.

The farm has a longer story than most. Documents in the county record office show that the upper fields were part of a medieval open field, and the long, gentle ridges that cross the western terrace are traces of old ploughing. A field name on a nineteenth-century map, Brack Furlong, gave the place its name, and the oak at the lane end appears on a survey from the 1840s. The farmhouse dates from the 1700s, with a barn added a century later. In the twentieth century the land was grazed by a dairy herd, and a small orchard stood where the new trees will go. A local historian has agreed to help us write a short guide to the site's past, with old photographs from villagers. The archaeologist who visited the barn found nothing that would stop our plans, but asked us to report any finds such as pottery or coins. We think this story adds meaning to the project, and we will put a panel by the gate so that every visitor can read it. The finds, if any, will be handed to the county museum for safe keeping.

Dry summers are becoming common in the district, so the crop plan has been adjusted for resilience. We will favour varieties known to cope with heat and patchy rain, such as Florence fennel, chard, winter squash, dwarf French beans and drought-tolerant herbs like thyme, rosemary and sage. Sowing dates are chosen to bring crops through their thirstiest stage in the cooler, wetter part of the year: spinach and peas are sown early, leeks and kale are planted in the damper days of June, and carrots are sown in two flushes to avoid a poor germination in the heat of July. Deep-rooted crops are placed on the lighter terrace where they can reach moisture lower down, and shallow-rooted salads sit by the tank where the beds are cool. We have dropped crops that need constant moisture, such as celery and celeriac, from the first year's list. If a prolonged drought is forecast, the head grower may sow a late green manure instead of a vegetable crop, so that the soil is covered and effort is not wasted on plants that cannot be kept alive.

Produce goes from the field to a covered wash station within thirty minutes of cutting. The station has two stainless sinks, a draining rack and a hose with a clean-water supply, and leaves are dunked, rinsed and spun dry in a salad spinner before packing. Roots are brushed and rinsed on a slatted table. Anything perishable then moves straight into a walk-in cold store converted from a shipping container, held at 4 degrees Celsius with a thermometer alarm. Salad leaves and herbs are kept there for no more than three days, soft fruit for two days, and brassicas and courgettes for about five. Hardier crops use other methods. Potatoes, onions and squash are cured in the dry loft for two weeks, then stored in the cool, dark cellar at 8 degrees, where they last through the winter. Carrots and beetroot go into clamps of damp sand in the cellar, and apples are laid on slatted trays, each wrapped lightly in paper. Each crate carries a date label, and a first-in, first-out rule applies. The cellar is checked weekly, and any softening produce is removed.

The four vegetable plots will follow a strict four-year rotation, so each family returns to the same ground only once every fourth year. Plot one starts with legumes, meaning peas and beans, which leave nitrogen in the soil. In year two it carries brassicas, hungry feeders that use that nitrogen and need the firm ground the beans left behind. Year three is roots and alliums, carrots, beetroot, parsnips, onions and garlic, which do best in soil that has not been recently manured. Year four brings the solanums and cucurbits, potatoes, tomatoes and squash, which receive the year's heavy compost. Then the cycle begins again with legumes. The other three plots are staggered by one year each, so that every family grows somewhere every season. A table on the shed wall shows the plan for the next four years, with each plot and family in its own colour. Because potatoes and tomatoes share blight, they are never placed next to each other, and the brassica plot is always lime-dressed ahead of planting to help guard against clubroot. Any change is entered in the record book.

Because school groups and a weekly session for adults with learning disabilities will use the site, we have adopted a written safeguarding policy that every trustee has signed. The trustee who chairs our welfare group, the Trust's treasurer, acts as designated safeguarding lead, with the coordinator as deputy; both have completed a recognised two-day course within the past year. Anyone who will be left alone with children or vulnerable adults, whether paid or unpaid, must obtain an enhanced criminal records check through the county voluntary services umbrella body before they start, and checks are renewed every three years. Volunteers are never permitted to be alone with a child in a closed space, and school pupils are always accompanied by their own teachers. A worried volunteer should tell the lead immediately, or the deputy if the lead is the subject of the concern, and write down what they saw and heard in plain words. The lead decides within a day whether to refer the matter to the local authority's children or adult services, and records the decision. We do not investigate allegations ourselves. A summary card with the reporting numbers hangs in the shed, and the policy is reviewed each year.

Good organisation depends on having clear roles, and the Trust has worked hard to define them. The secretary looks after correspondence, prepares agendas and takes minutes at every meeting. The treasurer keeps the accounts, pays bills and prepares the annual report. The coordinator, once appointed, will run the day to day programme and supervise volunteers, reporting to the chair. Each working group has a convenor who organises its tasks and keeps the others informed. Written role descriptions, no more than a page each, are given to anyone who takes on a post, and are reviewed whenever the post changes hands. We have found that people are far more willing to step forward when they know exactly what is expected and how much time it will take. At the March gathering, the roles are listed with the names of those who hold them, and any member is welcome to ask about taking one on. A deputy is named for each of the three main officers, to ensure that the work continues when someone is ill or away. The constitution also sets out how a vacancy is filled between annual gatherings, so that no post remains empty for long.

The roofs are the first problem to fix, because the guttering at Brackenfold Farm has been failing for years. The long barn sheds its rain onto the cobbled yard, where it has pooled against the north wall and loosened the lime mortar. We will replace the rotted cast gutters with half-round aluminium ones and fit a downpipe at each corner, then connect them to the existing storm drain in the lane, which the council has confirmed has spare capacity. The pipe runs are laid at a fall of one in eighty so that leaves and grit flush through instead of settling. Every downpipe gets a removable leaf guard, and the stewards will clear them each October and again after the first big storm of spring. We will also regrade the yard by about three centimetres across its width so that nothing runs back toward the barn wall. The aim is simply to move heavy rain away from the buildings quickly and without scouring the track. A local drainage contractor has surveyed the levels, agreed the layout and promised to finish before the autumn rains, so the barn can then be used for seed drying and workshops.

We propose to report to the funder four times a year for the first eighteen months and twice a year thereafter, always within thirty days of the end of the period covered. The quarterly reports will be short, no more than three pages, and will contain a narrative of activity, a table of spending against the approved budget, an updated list of risks and any changes we are asking the funder to accept. The two later reports will be fuller, adding attendance figures, case studies and photographs, and the final report at the end of the third year will include the independent evaluator's findings and a statement of what has been learned. The coordinator drafts each report, the treasurer checks every figure, and the chair signs it on behalf of the trustees after reading it at a board meeting. A copy is placed on the Trust's website and in the hall for any member to read. We will contact the funder's officer in advance if we expect a deadline to be missed, and will welcome a visit at any time. A reporting calendar showing the due dates has been added to the shared diary used by the coordinator and the treasurer.

Picking is planned to the day. The head grower draws up a harvest list on Sunday evening, based on what is ready and what has been ordered, and pins it to the shed door. Salad and soft fruit are harvested first thing, before the sun warms the leaves, and heavy crops like squash and potatoes are lifted in the afternoon when the ground is dry. A crew of four, led by the site lead, works in pairs along the beds, with one person cutting and the other carrying crates to the shade. Knives are sharp and washed between beds. We use lightweight stackable crates that are not overfilled, since bruising damages quality, and leaves are laid loosely, not packed. Pickers are shown how to recognise ripeness for each crop, such as the sheen on a courgette or the hollow sound of a ripe squash, so that nothing is cut too early or left to turn tough. At the end of each session, the crew weighs the day's list against what was picked and notes shortfalls. Spare tools and gloves are kept in a bucket at the end of each plot.

The lowest plot, nearest the stream, stands under water for weeks in a wet winter, and we will address it with a combination of drainage and raised ground. A new ditch, a metre wide and 60 centimetres deep, will be re-cut along the northern boundary and will fall gently to the stream through a stone-lined outlet. Inside the plot, a herringbone of perforated land drains, laid in gravel trenches 80 centimetres deep and 8 metres apart, will carry excess water to the ditch. Where the ground is still too wet, we will build the beds up as raised mounds 30 centimetres high, made from the soil dug out of the ditch and topped with compost. The lowest corner will be left as a small wet meadow with sedges and marsh marigolds rather than drained. Outlets are fitted with a flap to prevent stream water running back in when it rises. A contractor will dig the drains in early autumn, and the ditch will be cleared each October. We will measure the success of the work by noting how long water stands on the surface after heavy rain.

Before any earth is moved, we need to know exactly what shape the land has. A surveyor will walk the site with a GPS receiver and a laser level and produce a contour map at fifty-centimetre intervals, showing every rise, hollow and flow path. The map will mark the gradient in four bands, from gentle to steep, and show where water currently runs during storms. Findings so far suggest that the upper field averages one in eight, the middle field one in twenty and the lower field is almost flat. We will also record the position of the existing field drain, the spring beside the hedge and the lowest point where water gathers. The final survey will be drawn on a base plan and kept in the shed, with a copy sent to the funder. Volunteers will be shown how to read the contours so that they can understand why some beds dry more slowly than others. The data forms the basis for every design decision, but the survey itself changes nothing on the ground. It is scheduled for the first fortnight of the project.

The Trust is governed by a board of nine trustees. Seven are elected by the membership at the annual gathering each March, standing for a term of three years, with one third of the seats coming up every year so that experience is never lost entirely. No trustee may serve more than two consecutive terms, though they may stand again after a year away. The remaining two seats are held by representatives nominated by Marlowe Reach Parish Council and by the Ashcombe High School governing body, each appointed for one year at a time and renewable. The board must always include a chair, a secretary and a treasurer, who are chosen by the trustees from among themselves at their first meeting after the annual gathering. Nominations are open to any member aged sixteen or over, and a candidate needs a proposer and a seconder. We aim for a spread of skills, and the board reviews each year whether it needs someone with legal, financial, or building experience. At least three trustees must be under forty, a rule we adopted to keep the board in touch with younger residents. The coordinator attends meetings but has no vote. The full details are set out in clauses six to nine of our constitution.

Deer and rabbits are the main browsers around Hollowmere, and we will fence them out rather than rely on repellents. The growing area and orchard will be enclosed with a 1.8-metre fence of galvanised woven wire on chestnut posts set three metres apart, tall enough to deter roe deer, which can clear one and a half metres from a standing start. The bottom 40 centimetres is bent outward and pegged flat, or buried 30 centimetres deep, to stop rabbits digging under, and the mesh near the ground is small enough, at 30 millimetres, to exclude them. Gates are the same height and hang on self-closing hinges, with a second gate forming an airlock at the main entrance. The hedge planted along the outside will, in time, thicken the barrier. Individual young trees in the outer fields get a spiral guard and a 120-centimetre cane tube against nibbling. We will walk the fence line every Monday, patch any damage, and trim vegetation that touches the wire. A contractor will build the fence in the first autumn, before the deer find the new crops.

Learning is one of the pleasures of working in a group, and we try to make room for it. Experienced members often share what they know informally while working alongside newcomers, passing on tips about everything from sharpening a spade to reading the weather. Once a season we arrange an evening talk in the village hall, open to everyone, where a guest speaker from the county wildlife group or the regional records office shares their knowledge. These evenings are popular, with an average attendance of forty, and the audience often asks questions for longer than the talk itself. We also keep a small lending library in the shed, with books on local history, hedgerows and traditional crafts, and the youth group has produced a scrapbook of photographs and stories from past work days. Members have suggested that they would enjoy a day trip to see similar schemes elsewhere, and the committee has agreed to organise one each summer, paid for by fundraising rather than from the grant, so that anyone who wants to broaden their experience can do so. Several members have said these informal exchanges taught them more than any formal course, and we hope to keep that generous habit alive.

Moving seedlings from sheltered conditions to open ground is a delicate step, and we have a routine for it. About ten days before planting out, trays are carried each morning to a cold frame beside the tunnel and left with the lid propped open, then closed again at night. The lid is propped wider every other day, and in the final three days the trays stay out overnight under fleece. This hardening off toughens the leaves and slows soft growth that would otherwise scorch in sun or snap in wind. Transplanting happens in the evening or on a cloudy day to reduce shock. Each seedling is lifted by its leaf, never by the stem, and set in a hole that has been watered beforehand and firmed gently around the roots. Brassicas are planted slightly deeper than they were in the tray, to give stability, while onions and leeks are dropped into dibbed holes and left to settle with a gentle trickle. Any gaps are filled from a reserve tray of spare plants held back for exactly that purpose. A simple checklist hangs in the tunnel as a reminder of each step for new volunteers.

A thorough work plan sits behind our application, and we are confident that it can be delivered. The first six months will be spent on preparation, with the appointment of the coordinator, finalising the contracts and holding public consultation events. Building work on the hall and the main path is scheduled to start in the second spring and finish before the autumn, so that the site is fully usable by the end of the first year. Years two and three will focus on bringing in new visitors and volunteers, setting up the schools programme and building up the sources of income that will sustain the Trust. A detailed timeline in the form of a chart is attached as Annex B, and shows each activity, its start and end, who will carry it out and what must have been done before it can begin. We have been realistic about what is achievable and have allowed longer for tasks that depend on others. The trustees have agreed that if the schedule slips, the coordinator will tell them at once so that a decision can be taken.

Our pesticide policy is short and firm: no synthetic insecticides, molluscicides or herbicides will be bought, stored or used anywhere on the site, and this applies to volunteers, contractors and visitors as well. The policy is written on a laminated page inside the shed door, and each new volunteer signs to say they have read it. A locked cupboard holds the only products permitted on the farm, which are sulphur dust for the rare mildew outbreak and a small bottle of potassium soap, both of which sit on the national list of approved organic inputs. Any use of these is logged with the date, the bed, the quantity and the reason, and the head grower must sign every entry. Labels are kept with the containers, and empty containers go to the household hazardous waste point at the recycling centre. Neighbouring farms have been told about our policy, and we have asked them to warn us before any spraying near our boundary. We will also check seed, plug plants and compost from suppliers for any treatment claims before accepting delivery. Visitors are reminded of the rule on the sign at the gate.

Composting happens in a row of three timber bays at the top of the market garden, each one two metres wide and deep and one and a half metres high. Boards slide into grooves at the front so we can build up the heap and still reach the base. Fresh material goes into the first bay, which we turn into the second after three weeks and into the third after another three, so that every batch passes through a full hot phase and a long cooling phase. A fourth, smaller bay holds browns such as straw and shredded cardboard. Each bay has a lid of old pallets and a roof of corrugated sheet to stop rain from drowning the heap. Our estimate is that the system will handle about eight tonnes of green waste a year, drawn from our own trimmings, spoiled crops and kitchen scraps from the village hall. That would yield around four tonnes of finished compost, enough to put two centimetres across all four plots. Bays are filled and emptied on a rota posted in the shed, and the site lead weighs each load coming in so we can check the real tonnage against this forecast.

Every receipt, invoice, bank statement and signed timesheet is scanned by the treasurer within a week of arriving and filed in a dated folder on the Trust's shared drive, with the paper original stored in a lockable cabinet in the hall office. The ledger is kept in a simple accounting package that produces a monthly trial balance, and a photograph record of each completed piece of work is added to the project file with the date and location. We will keep all financial papers for seven years after the end of the grant period, which is longer than the law requires, and minutes and signed agreements for as long as the Trust exists. Records relating to grant spending will be marked so that they can be found quickly. The funder's staff and auditors may inspect any of these records at any time on reasonable notice, and so may the charity regulator, our independent examiner and the parish council under the terms of the lease. Members may look at the accounts and minutes on request to the secretary. Backups of the shared drive are taken weekly to an external disk held at the treasurer's home, and a second copy is stored offsite in the cloud.

During the first two seasons we will run small variety trials to find out which crops genuinely suit our heavy, late-draining ground. Each trial compares three varieties of one crop, such as carrots, planted side by side in a single bed in identical conditions and given the same care. Volunteers record the date each variety germinates, how many plants survive, how long it takes to reach picking size and how it tastes in a blind cooking session. Photographs are taken at fixed points every fortnight. At the end of the season the scores are added up on a simple chart, and the winner earns a bigger share of the following year's plantings. We are especially interested in how varieties cope with a cold, wet May, since that is when the valley floor tends to lose seedlings. Results will be shared with other growers in the district through a short note and a stall at the spring open day. The trials cost little, and they give the team a practical way to learn which choices pay off. Winners and losers are written up honestly, because a failed variety teaches us as much as a successful one does.

Mulch only works if there is enough of it, and getting a steady supply is a project in its own right. Our main source will be a local tree surgery firm that currently pays to dispose of wood chip, and which has agreed to deliver loads of about eight cubic metres at no charge whenever it is working within ten miles. We expect to take between six and ten loads in the first year. Straw will come from a neighbouring arable farm in September, bought in small bales at a fair price, and leaf mould from the council's park-keepers each November. Deliveries are tipped on a hard apron at the field gate, where the chip is left to age for at least two months so that it does not rob the soil of nitrogen. A tarpaulin covers the heaps in winter to keep them from drying out or soaking through. The site lead will check each load for plastic, treated timber and walnut or laurel leaves, and refuse any that fails. A stockpile log notes volumes in and out. We also keep a small reserve of cardboard collected from local shops.

Volunteers are the backbone of the Trust, and we are conscious of how much we ask of them. Last year, sixty-three people gave at least one session, and fourteen of them came every week. Between them they contributed an estimated 2,900 hours, which at the minimum wage rate would be worth well over twenty thousand pounds. We keep a register of attendance at every work day and thank people publicly at the annual meeting, where long-serving members receive a small certificate. A summer picnic and a winter supper are held for all volunteers and their families, paid for from the fete proceeds. We recognise that regular volunteers can become tired, so we encourage a rota that lets people step back without feeling guilty, and the coordinator telephones anyone who has missed three sessions in a row, simply to check they are well. The average length of service among our current volunteers is just over four years, which we regard as a sign that people enjoy what they do. We would like to keep this loyalty while also welcoming new faces as the project grows.

We have chosen five measures that we can actually collect. First, the number of different people attending a session each month: the baseline is 63 over the last year, and we aim for 140 by the end of year two, counted from the attendance register. Second, weekly volunteer hours, now averaging 55 and targeted at 120, taken from the same register. Third, the share of participants who live within the three poorest neighbourhoods of Ashcombe, which stands at 9 per cent and which we want to raise to 25 per cent, based on postcodes given voluntarily on sign-up. Fourth, the proportion of regular participants who report feeling less lonely, measured with a three-question survey at joining, at six months and at twelve months; we have no baseline yet, so the first intake will set one, and we will aim for two thirds reporting improvement. Fifth, the number of school pupils visiting each year, currently 90 and targeted at 400, taken from booking records. The coordinator will collate the figures every quarter, and an external evaluator will review them and interview twenty participants in the final year, so that the numbers are supported by people's own accounts.

We have already made a number of purchases for the Trust and have built up good relationships with local suppliers. Our tools come from the family-run hardware shop in Ashcombe, which gives us a discount of ten per cent and lets us pay at the end of the month. Timber for benches and signs is bought from the sawmill at Harrowgate Fold, and delivered on the back of a farmer's trailer. The printer who produces our leaflets is a member of the Trust, and she charges us at cost. Because the businesses are small and local, we can ring them up for advice, and we are often able to collect things the same day. We believe that spending money in the area is one way in which the project can benefit the wider community, and several of the shopkeepers have told us they are delighted to be involved. When we expand the programme, we plan to continue to buy as much as we can from local firms, and we will tell them in advance about our larger orders. We keep a list of the local firms we use, with their contact details and what they supply, in the shed, so that any trustee can place an order quickly.

The tool store is the one building we must construct before anything else, so we have given it careful thought. It will be a timber-framed shed measuring six metres by three, built on a concrete pad, with a pitched roof of corrugated steel and a lean-to at the side for wheelbarrows. The walls are lined with plywood panels to take hooks and shelves, and two small windows with security mesh give daylight. Floor level is raised fifteen centimetres to keep out damp, and the doorway is wide enough for the walking tractor to enter. A local joiner has quoted for the frame, and volunteers will help with cladding and painting under his guidance. Planning officers have confirmed that no permission is needed, since the structure is below the size limit for outbuildings. We have also marked a space near the door for a hand-washing station and a bench for repairs. Construction is expected to take three weeks in early spring, and the building will serve as a dry shelter during storms. A small bench vice and a grinding wheel will be fixed at one end, so that simple repairs can be done indoors and in comfort even when it rains.

Seedlings will be raised in a dedicated propagation area built into the south end of a new polytunnel. The tunnel measures eight metres by four, giving 32 square metres under cover, of which 10 square metres is reserved for trays on two tiers of slatted benches at waist height. Heat comes from electrically warmed mats under the trays, controlled by a thermostat set at 18 degrees for germination, and the benches are enclosed by a second layer of clear fleece on cold nights. We have chosen low-wattage mats because the site has a limited power supply, and a small solar panel on the barn roof will charge the battery that runs them in daytime. The tunnel is ventilated through automatic roof vents that open on a wax cylinder as the temperature climbs past 22 degrees, together with roll-up sides and a door at each end. A max-min thermometer hangs at bench height, and the site lead reads it every morning and again at dusk. Trays are raised off the floor to avoid damp, and the benches are scrubbed each winter to prevent disease.

Produce leaves the site in sturdy, reusable crates lined with a clean cloth, and is taken to the village market and to local households in a small electric van borrowed from a neighbour. Salad bags are replaced by waxed cotton bags that customers return, and loose vegetables go in paper. Each crate carries a label with the crop, the harvest date and the plot it came from, so that a problem can be traced. The load is packed at the shed in the order it will be delivered, and heavy items such as potatoes go at the bottom, with delicate leaves on top. On warm days, the van is parked in shade and a cool box with frozen packs travels with the most perishable items. Drivers aim to deliver within three hours of leaving the shed and to return unsold produce directly to the compost bays. We expect to make two deliveries a week in season, on Wednesday and Saturday. A delivery sheet is signed by the person receiving the crates, which are collected clean on the next round. Returned crates are scrubbed in the wash station before they are used again.

To plan the beds and the budget, we need an idea of how much the site should produce. Using published figures for market gardens in similar climates, and discounting them by a third because we are new, we estimate an output of about 1.5 kilograms of vegetables per square metre of bed in the first year, rising to 2.5 kilograms by the third. With 3,000 square metres of beds in production, that means roughly 4.5 tonnes in year one and 7.5 in year three. Salad crops and courgettes are expected to give the highest weight per metre, while garlic and onions give the least. We have split the forecast by month, assuming that the heaviest weeks fall in August and September, and have used it to size the cold store, the number of crates and the staffing of the harvest crew. The estimate rests on assumptions about weather and pest losses, which are stated in the annex, and it will be revised in the light of experience. The projections are not a promise, but a working figure to plan around.

We learned a great deal from the first small project we ran, a path restoration in the second year of the Trust, which cost 9,000 and finished a month late. Two things went wrong: the weather was wetter than forecast, and the volunteer group underestimated how long the edging would take. The experience was frustrating at the time, but it taught us to add a margin to every timetable, to agree start dates with contractors only after checking the long range forecast, and to ask experienced people to check our estimates. It also taught us that open communication is better than silence: when we told neighbours in advance about the delay, none of them complained. We have written a short lessons learned note for every project since, and the trustees read these before beginning anything new. We think this habit of looking back honestly is one of our strengths, and we have shared our notes with two other groups in the area who wanted to follow our example. The note from the path project is kept in the hall office and has been consulted by two other groups since.

The upper field falls at about one in eight toward the stream, and in heavy rain the surface has already been carried away in rills. We will tackle this with a set of simple earthworks and plantings that slow and spread the flow. Three contour swales, shallow ditches dug along the line of the slope and planted with a berm of fruit bushes on their lower lip, will intercept running water and let it soak in. Between the swales, the beds are laid out across the slope instead of down it, so each row acts as a small dam. A twelve-metre-wide band of permanent grass and willow whips is left along the stream edge to filter any sediment that does escape. Winter cover crops of rye and vetch hold bare ground between harvests, and a narrow terrace faced with stacked timber will carry the main path where the slope is steepest. Our contractor will set out the contours with a laser level, and the swales are checked after each storm. We expect the system to keep silt out of the stream and to raise the amount of moisture stored in the upper beds.

A young tree has little chance unless it is looked after in its first three summers, so we have planned that care closely. Each planting hole is dug wide and shallow, and the roots are spread out and backfilled with the original soil rather than rich compost, which discourages roots from circling. Every tree gets a stake on the windward side, a rubber tie and a spiral guard against voles and rabbits. A mulch mat of cardboard and wood chip, around a metre across, suppresses grass without touching the trunk. During the first two summers volunteers water each tree with twenty litres every ten days when there is no rain. A walk each autumn checks ties, which are loosened as trunks thicken, and replaces any dead tree in the following winter. We will keep a record of survival in each block so we can see whether the soil or the wind is taking a toll. Formative pruning begins in the second winter, and by year four we expect to remove stakes and guards. A leaflet for volunteers explains each job with pictures.

The trustees keep a risk register, reviewed at every second board meeting, and the five entries that matter most are these. Contractor delay on the hall refit is rated medium for likelihood and high for impact; the chair owns it, and the contract includes a retention of five per cent until completion. Loss of the coordinator, again medium likelihood and high impact, is owned by the secretary, who will keep a trained deputy and a handover folder. A shortfall in volunteers is rated high likelihood but low impact, since core tasks can be paced to suit, and the volunteer lead is responsible for monitoring numbers monthly. Cost rises in materials are medium and medium, held by the treasurer, who will draw on the contingency and renegotiate scope if it is exhausted. Finally, delay in obtaining planning consent for the new entrance is low likelihood but high impact; the coordinator has already held a pre-application meeting with the district council. Each risk shows a score from one to nine, the action planned and the date by which it will be next examined. Any risk scoring seven or more is reported to the funder in the next quarterly update, together with the steps we are taking.

For about forty years the lower half of the site was a vehicle repair yard, with a concrete forecourt, an inspection pit and an oil tank, before it was left derelict. Because of this, we commissioned a desk study that traced old maps and trade directories, followed by a walkover survey and soil sampling at 30 points on a grid. The laboratory found lead at up to 410 milligrams per kilogram and hydrocarbons near the old pit, both above safe levels for growing food. We therefore removed the concrete, dug out the contaminated pit area and a 30-centimetre layer of topsoil across the worst zone, and disposed of it through a licensed carrier. The cleared ground was lined with a geotextile membrane and capped with 40 centimetres of clean certified topsoil. A follow-up test of the new surface showed lead below 60 milligrams per kilogram. Leafy and root crops will be grown only in the capped area and in raised beds there. The council's environmental health team reviewed the report and confirmed in writing that the land is suitable for the use. Reports are attached as Appendix H.

Disease is the other half of crop protection, and in our humid valley, fungal problems like potato blight and downy mildew can wipe out a bed in days. Our approach is to stop the conditions that favour them. Plants are spaced generously so that air moves between leaves, and watering is done at the base in the morning so foliage dries before night. We will choose varieties with a known tolerance, such as blight-resistant tomatoes and mildew-tolerant spinach, and rotate crop families so that spores in the soil starve between hosts. Infected leaves are removed at the first sign of spotting and bagged for the hot compost rather than the open heap. Tools are wiped with a cloth and diluted disinfectant between beds. In the tunnel, doors and side vents are opened early on mild days. Blight forecasts from the national weather service are checked each week from June, and potatoes are lifted early if conditions turn dangerous. Records of each outbreak go in the grower's notebook with the date, weather and what we did, so that we learn from each season.

The site includes a tool container, a stock of wood chip and several thousand pounds of equipment, so we have given thought to keeping the place secure when no one is there. The gate at the lane will have a heavy-duty padlock and a sliding bolt, and the container is fitted with a steel hasp and a disc lock. A solar-powered floodlight with a motion sensor lights the yard after dark, and a simple sign states that the site is monitored. Neighbours on the lane have our phone numbers and have agreed to report anything unusual. We do not plan to use razor wire or spikes, since this is a community space and we want it to feel welcoming. Instead, a low timber post-and-rail fence marks the boundary, and the barn door is made of oak battens that are hard to break. A short log in the shed records any incident, however small, and the committee reviews it every quarter. The insurer has examined the arrangements and confirmed that they meet the cover requirements. The barn roof is fitted with a lockable skylight, so that nothing valuable is left visible from the lane.

Where our trees come from matters as much as how we plant them. All stock will be bought from nurseries that hold plant health certification and grow native species from seed collected within a hundred miles, because trees of local origin cope better with our climate and carry fewer imported pests. We will refuse any consignment with signs of canker, root rot or insect damage, and the delivery will be inspected by two people on arrival. Bare-root trees are ordered for delivery in late November, when the plants are dormant and the soil is still warm enough for roots to settle, and are heeled into a trench of damp sand if the ground is frozen. The nursery will provide a passport for each batch so that a plant disease outbreak could be traced. Planting is aimed for the first fortnight of December, with a fallback date in February. Container trees are avoided, as they tend to hold roots in a tight coil. The head grower will visit the nursery in October to choose the best stock, and photographs will be taken of everything we receive.

We believe that no organisation can achieve much alone, and we try to work closely with other groups in the valley. Our members include people from the Women's Institute, the history society, the cricket club, the church and the youth club, and several of them sit on our working groups. Joint events have been popular: last summer, the church and the cricket club helped us run a harvest supper for ninety people, and the history society produced a display of old photographs of the common. We also exchange news with similar groups in neighbouring villages, and two of our members visited a community orchard near Linnet Green to see how it manages its rota. These relationships are friendly and informal, and there are no contracts or formal obligations. We value the goodwill that comes from knowing people personally, and we think that the strength of a partnership lies in trust, not paperwork. In the future we hope to hold a yearly gathering of all the groups in the valley, to share plans and avoid clashes in the calendar. These friendships have already saved us money, since neighbouring groups lend marquees, trestle tables and a trailer whenever we ask.

Beds will be watered by drip lines rather than sprinklers, so that water goes straight to the roots and none is lost to wind or to leaves. Each bed carries two lines of pressure-compensating tape with emitters every 20 centimetres, fed from a manifold connected to the tank bank. A battery-powered timer opens the valves at 5:30 in the morning, when evaporation is lowest and the air is still. In a dry spell, we will irrigate established crops twice a week for forty minutes, which delivers about twenty millimetres of water, and newly planted seedlings daily for ten minutes until their roots take hold. Tomatoes and squash get a third session in the hottest weeks. A cheap soil probe pushed to a depth of ten centimetres tells the volunteer on duty whether the bed is truly dry before the timer is set. A hand-held watering can is used for seed trays and fussy salads only. Hoses are never run in the heat of the afternoon. At the end of each season the lines are flushed, drained and coiled in the shed, and any blocked emitter is replaced.

We are keen to learn from people who have done similar things before, and we have sought advice from several experienced organisations. A development worker from the county voluntary sector council has visited twice to look over our plans and has offered some helpful suggestions about our constitution and funding applications. An adviser from a regional network of community land groups ran a workshop for our trustees last winter, covering lease terms, health and safety and the legal duties of a charity. We have also been in touch with a larger trust in the next county that has managed a similar site for fifteen years, and its chair kindly gave us an afternoon of her time. None of these bodies is paid by us, and none has any formal role in our project. Their help has been generous and valuable, but we remain responsible for our own decisions. We plan to keep up these links, and have set aside a small amount in the budget so that two trustees can attend the regional network's annual conference each year. We are grateful for this goodwill, and we make a point of thanking each adviser in writing and inviting them to our open days.

Before choosing how to tackle weeds, we first carried out a survey of what is there. Over two afternoons in June, volunteers walked each plot in a grid and recorded the weed species they found, ranked from absent to dominant on a five-point scale. The western terrace is dominated by couch grass and creeping thistle, while the old garden plot is rich in chickweed, groundsel and dock. Bindweed has taken hold along the southern boundary fence. Each species was photographed and pressed in a book to help new volunteers learn them, and the survey sheets are stored in the shed. Knowing which weeds spread by roots and which by seed matters, because they behave differently under the hoe. Some species, such as chickweed and fat hen, are edible and may find their way into the kitchen. We will repeat the survey each June, and the changes should tell us whether our methods are shrinking the weed seed bank over time. A local botanist has agreed to check our identifications and add a note on any rare plants worth protecting. A copy goes to the grower for planning.

Understanding how wet the land really is will guide everything we do. Two shallow observation wells, made of perforated pipe sunk a metre into the ground, will be installed in the lowest plot and in the middle field, and each is fitted with a cap and a marked dipstick. The site lead will record the water level once a week, and daily after storms, and enter it in a notebook beside the rainfall figure. Over a couple of winters, these readings will show how high the water table rises and how quickly it falls. We also keep a flood diary in which volunteers record when and where water lies on the surface, with photographs. Old maps held in the county archive suggest that the lowest corner was once a pond that was filled in, and neighbours remember water standing there through the winter of two years ago. We will send our records to the local flood group, who are building a picture of groundwater across the valley. The data costs almost nothing but could save us from poor decisions. Readings will also help us decide whether further drains are needed.

The full request is 118,000 over three years, and every pound is assigned to one of six headings. Site works and fencing take 31,400, the community hall refit takes 24,800, and tools and equipment account for 9,600. Staff costs come to 36,200, covering a part-time coordinator at three days a week plus employer pension and national insurance contributions. Publicity, printing and translation of leaflets total 4,300, and an annual independent examination of the accounts adds 2,700. That leaves 9,000, which we have set aside as a contingency fund equal to roughly eight per cent of the total. We chose that figure after the quantity surveyor advised that small rural works commonly overrun by between five and ten per cent, and because two of our quotes are valid for only six months. The contingency can be spent only with the treasurer's written agreement and the funder's notification, and anything left over in the final quarter will be returned rather than reallocated. A full line by line spreadsheet, showing unit costs, quotations obtained and the year in which each item falls, forms Annex C. Inflation has been allowed for at three per cent a year on staff costs only, since the material prices are fixed in the quotes.

Volunteer wellbeing is something we think about carefully, particularly because many of our members are over sixty. Every session begins with a short briefing from the session leader, who explains the planned tasks, points out any hazards and reminds people to drink water and take breaks. Seating is placed at intervals around the site, and a first aid kit and a defibrillator are kept in the hall, which is never more than two minutes' walk away. In hot weather we move heavy tasks to the early morning, and in frosty weather we switch to indoor jobs such as repairing tools or sorting seed. The leader keeps a list of any medical conditions volunteers have chosen to share, and holds emergency contact numbers in a sealed envelope. If anyone is hurt, the incident is written into the accident book and reviewed by the trustees at their next meeting, so that we can learn from it. We have been fortunate to record only minor scrapes and one twisted ankle in the last five years, and we want to keep it that way.

Parts of the growing area will use imported soil, so we have written a specification to make sure it is fit for purpose. Raised beds will be filled with a blended topsoil that conforms to the national standard for general-purpose topsoil, with a stated range for pH, organic matter and particle size. The supplier must provide a certificate with each load, showing laboratory results for common contaminants including lead, arsenic and cadmium, and must tell us where the soil was dug. We will refuse any delivery that arrives without a certificate or that contains visible rubbish, large stones or roots of invasive weeds such as Japanese knotweed. The first load will be inspected by the site lead and a trained volunteer before it is tipped, and a sample from every fifth load is kept in a labelled jar in case a question arises later. The beds are lined at the bottom with a permeable membrane that stops weed roots from below. Each bed is filled to a depth of thirty centimetres, firmed lightly and left for a month to settle before planting.
